narration: You put a thousand dollars into your bank. In your head, it's sitting in a vault somewhere, your exact bills, waiting for you. It isn't. And that's the small shock.
The big shock is this. Almost all the money in the entire economy was never printed by any government. It was created, out of thin air, by ordinary banks.
In a modern economy, around ninety-seven percent of all money exists only as numbers in bank computers — conjured into being when banks make loans.
sub: of money is created by private banks

narration: Now, this isn't some dark conspiracy. It's not even a secret. It's simply how banking has worked for centuries — hidden in plain sight, inside the accounting.
Most people picture money being printed by the government. In reality, the lion's share is typed into being by your bank.
Most people assume money comes from a government printing press. The truth is far stranger, and it happens millions of times a day.
Because new money isn't mostly printed. It's typed — one keystroke at a time.
caption: most money is typed, not printed

narration: So where does money actually come from? Let's follow a single loan, and watch money appear — and later vanish — right in front of us.
heading: How Banks Create Money From Nothing
sub: It isn't printed. It's lent into existence.

narration: Start with the story we all believe. The bank is a middleman. Savers put money in, the bank lends that same money out to borrowers. A sensible pass-through.
It's tidy, intuitive, and taught everywhere. It's also, in a crucial way, wrong.
memeBottom: banks don't lend out your savings

narration: Here's how the Bank of England itself describes it. Commercial banks don't just move existing money — they create it.
This trick is ancient. Centuries ago, goldsmiths stored people's gold and handed out paper receipts for it. Soon they noticed something: people almost never came to collect the actual gold.
caption: it started with goldsmiths

narration: So the goldsmiths quietly wrote more paper receipts than they had gold, and lent them out. Those receipts circulated as money. Banking had discovered it could create claims on money it didn't really hold.
A commercial bank takes deposits and makes loans. But the loan doesn't come out of a pile of savings in the back.
When a bank grants you a loan, it simply types a new number into your account. That deposit didn't come from anyone else. It's brand-new money.
caption: the loan creates the deposit

narration: Watch it on the bank's own books. Two entries appear at once: your loan, which you owe them, and your deposit, which they owe you.
caption: two entries, one click

narration: Before you walked in, that money did not exist. The instant the loan is approved, it does. The bank didn't move money — it manufactured it.
If your gut says 'that feels like cheating,' you're not wrong to flinch. But it's also the engine that builds houses, factories and businesses before anyone has saved up the money for them.
And this is why hardly any of it is physical. Only a tiny sliver of all the money out there is actual cash.
caption: 3% cash · 97% digits

narration: The vast majority of the money supply is just deposits — numbers in accounts, created by banks typing them in.
And that number sitting in your banking app? It isn't cash the bank is holding for you. It's an IOU — the bank's promise to hand you cash if you ever ask.
caption: your balance is an IOU

narration: Which is why your 'deposit' shows up as a liability on the bank's books. They owe it to you. Your asset is literally their debt.
If that sounds abstract, let's make it concrete. Let's buy a house.
heading: Follow One Mortgage

narration: You're approved for a three-hundred-thousand-dollar mortgage. The bank doesn't go find three hundred thousand in savings. It types it into your account.
caption: $300,000 — created on the spot

narration: In that single moment, the total money in the economy just went up by three hundred thousand dollars. Created by a loan.
You pay the seller. They bank the money. It moves from account to account — but at every step, it stays as deposits in the system. The new money is real, and it circulates.
caption: the new money flows through the economy

narration: And it isn't only mortgages. A business loan, a car loan, even a swipe of credit on a card — each one can spin up fresh deposits in exactly the same way.
caption: even a card swipe can create it

narration: That's the genuinely useful magic of it. A loan lets a factory get built, or a business get off the ground today — with money that only exists because someone believed it would be paid back.
So a loan doesn't shuffle old money around. It genuinely adds new money to the world. Which raises an obvious, slightly unsettling question.
Here's the other half almost nobody mentions. When you repay the loan, that money doesn't go into the bank's pocket. It disappears.
caption: repaying a loan destroys money

narration: The deposit the loan created is cancelled out against the loan as you pay it down. The money is un-created — destroyed, bit by bit, with every payment.
So what does the bank actually keep? The interest. That's the real prize — the money that doesn't vanish when the principal is repaid.
So money is constantly being born and dying. New loans create it. Repayments destroy it. The money supply is a living, breathing thing.
caption: money: created and destroyed, daily

narration: But here's a puzzle that quietly keeps economists up at night. If the loan only created the principal… where does the money to pay the interest come from?
The uncomfortable answer: from other loans, elsewhere in the system. For everyone's interest to be payable, the total pile of money and debt has to keep on growing.
caption: the interest comes from more debt

narration: Now, you may have heard a different version of this in school — fractional reserve banking. It's close, but it gets the order backwards.
heading: The Textbook vs Reality

narration: The classic story: banks keep only a fraction of deposits in reserve, and lend out the rest.
In that telling, one deposit lets the bank make a loan, which becomes a new deposit, which funds another loan — money multiplying as it ripples outward.
caption: the 'money multiplier'

narration: That ripple even has a name — the money multiplier — the ratio between all the bank money and the small base underneath it.
It's a useful picture. But modern central banks say the real causation runs the other way. Banks don't wait for deposits to lend.
They make the loan first — creating the deposit — and then find the reserves they need afterwards. Lending leads; reserves follow.
caption: loans come first, reserves after

narration: Reserve requirements still exist in many places — a minimum banks must hold — though some countries have now cut them to zero.
This reversed view even has a name: endogenous money. Money isn't dropped in from outside and multiplied — it's created from inside the economy, by the demand for loans.
Banks don't sit around waiting for savers. They chase good borrowers, lend first, and sort out the reserves later.
memeBottom: chasing new lending, not waiting for savings

narration: Which leads to the question everyone immediately asks. If banks can just type money into existence — why don't they create infinite money and keep it all?
heading: Why Not Infinite Money?

narration: It's the obvious temptation. If the printer is a keyboard, why ever stop typing?
The first limit is simple. A loan is only worth making if someone can pay it back. Banks need creditworthy borrowers — and there are only so many.
The second limit is risk. Every loan they create is a bet. Make too many bad ones, and the losses can wipe the bank out entirely.
The third is regulation. Banks must hold real capital — their own money at stake — behind the loans they make. That caps how much they can conjure.
caption: capital rules cap the printing

narration: And the fourth lever sits above them all: the central bank, which sets the price of money — the interest rate — and can cool the whole machine down.
caption: the central bank sets the rate

narration: So banks aren't free to print without limit. They're throttled by borrowers, by risk, by rules, and by the central bank. But within those limits — yes, they really do create money.
And you've watched all this slam into overdrive twice recently. In 2008, and again in 2020, central banks created trillions in brand-new money to stop the system from seizing up.
caption: 2008 & 2020: the printers roared

narration: Money that took centuries to build up was, in some cases, matched in a matter of weeks. Just numbers, typed into existence — at enormous scale.
sub: created in weeks during the crises

narration: So if commercial banks make most of the money, what exactly does the central bank do?
heading: The Central Bank

narration: The central bank runs the country's monetary policy — and it's the only one that issues physical cash and bank reserves.
Think of two kinds of money. The base money the central bank issues — cash and reserves — and the far larger pile of deposits the commercial banks create on top.
And in a crisis, the central bank can create money directly, buying up bonds on a massive scale. You've heard its name: quantitative easing.
So there are two money printers in the economy. A small, famous one at the central bank — and a vast, quiet one spread across every commercial bank.
caption: two printers: one loud, one quiet

narration: And the quiet one dwarfs the loud one. The overwhelming majority of money in your economy was created by private banks making loans.
title: Who actually creates the money

narration: Notice what that means for control. When banks lend eagerly, the money supply balloons. When they get scared and stop, it can actually shrink — sometimes faster than anyone wants.
That's part of what makes a credit crunch so brutal. It isn't just that loans stop — it's that the creation of money itself grinds to a halt.
caption: lending freezes → money dries up

narration: Now, a system where money is privately created out of debt has a few obvious cracks. Let's look at where it breaks.
heading: Where It Breaks

narration: First, booms. When banks lend freely, they're pumping new money straight into the economy — and often straight into asset prices.
caption: easy lending inflates bubbles

narration: That fresh money can chase houses, stocks, and crypto, inflating bubbles. And when the lending stops, the money creation stops with it — and the bubble deflates.
Second, the run. Because banks only hold a sliver of actual cash, they physically cannot hand everyone their money back at once.
A bank can create deposits with a keystroke — but it cannot create cash. So if everyone demands cash at the same time, even a healthy bank can collapse.
caption: the one thing a keystroke can't do

narration: We watched a modern version in 2023. A large US bank hit an online bank run — billions yanked out in hours, by phone — and collapsed almost overnight.
Which is why governments step in with a safety net: deposit insurance, promising your savings are protected even if the bank fails.
Deposit insurance plus a central bank willing to lend in an emergency does one job above all: it keeps you calm, so you never start the run in the first place.
And third, inflation. If banks create money far faster than the economy makes real goods, you get more dollars chasing the same stuff — and prices climb.
caption: too much money → inflation

narration: All of which makes people ask the big question: does money HAVE to be created as private debt? A handful of economists argue it doesn't.
Some propose 'sovereign money' — where only the central bank creates money, directly, and banks go back to being genuine middlemen. It's radical, contested, and still mostly theoretical.
caption: could the state create it instead?

narration: It's part of why crypto was dreamed up in the first place — a bid to build money that no bank and no government can simply conjure.
Whether crypto actually solved the trust problem, or just quietly moved it somewhere else, is a whole other story — one we've told on this channel.
So step back and look at what money actually is. It's stranger, and more fragile, than it looks.
heading: So What Is Money?

narration: Here's the part that quietly rearranges your brain. Almost every dollar in existence is there because someone, somewhere, took out a loan.
Money and debt are two sides of the same keystroke. If every loan on Earth were repaid tomorrow, almost all the money would simply disappear.
And none of it is backed by gold or silver anymore. It's fiat money — valuable purely because we all agree it is.
Fiat money works for one reason above all: the government accepts it for taxes and declares it legal tender — so everybody else takes it too.
So the whole thing floats on the same thing every episode on this channel keeps circling back to: trust.
caption: it all runs on trust

narration: Trust that your deposit is really there. Trust that the bank is good for it. Trust that the number on your screen will still buy groceries tomorrow.
So here's the whole strange truth in four lines. Banks create money when they lend. They destroy it when you repay. Almost all of it is debt. And all of it runs on trust.
lines: all of it runs on trust

narration: It isn't a fixed pile of gold in a vault. It's a vast, humming web of promises — created, destroyed, and re-created every single day.
And that web of promises isn't evil. It's how a modern economy funds its future before the money for it exists. But it's fragile — because it only holds while the trust holds.
So the honest answer to 'where does money come from' is unsettling and simple. Mostly, from a bank, deciding to type it in.
So the next time someone says the government prints all the money, you'll know the quieter truth. Most of it is printed by banks — one loan, one keystroke at a time.
